Arduino · Uno R3 · Lab 13

Matrix Keypads and Menu Input

Turn sixteen small switches into a clear, dependable practice snack menu.

Lab MaterialPracticePractice Quiz

What you will learn

  • Trace a row-and-column scan without an external keypad library.
  • Generate one event per stable press and require a stable release.
  • Separate selecting, confirming and cancelling a menu choice.

On your bench

  • Arduino Uno R3 and USB cable
  • Passive 4×4 matrix keypad, either membrane or button board, with its supplier pinout
  • Jumper wires and an adapter/breadboard suitable for its connector

Meet the components

Recognise the parts in the photos, then follow the labelled task diagrams for connections.

Before you build

  • Upload one complete sketch at a time and use Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. Disconnect USB before rewiring; D0/D1 remain free for USB Serial.
  • Identify R1–R4 and C1–C4 from the actual keypad documentation or an unpowered continuity check. Connector order varies; leave unused pads unconnected. A passive matrix keypad does not need a separate 5V or GND lead; all eight matrix conductors go to the assigned GPIO pins.
  • Rows R1–R4 run top to bottom: 1 2 3 A / 4 5 6 B / 7 8 9 C / * 0 # D. Columns C1–C4 run left to right. These are functional names, not ribbon-pin numbers.
  • Use one key at a time. These sketches reject scans with multiple detected contacts, but do not implement multi-key rollover. Diode-less matrices can produce ghost connections when several keys are held. This is a classroom menu, not access-control or payment equipment.

Copy one task’s sketch into Arduino IDE at a time. Replace the previous sketch before uploading the next example.

1. Matrix Scanning2. Debounced Press Events3. Coordinate Mapping4. Events Versus Repeated Levels5. Digit Characters and Available Values6. Bounded Numeric Entry7. Context-Dependent Menus8. Recovery and Input Traces

Matrix Scanning

Task 1 · Guided build

Locate each menu key

Each key joins one row conductor to one column conductor. Sixteen keys therefore need eight connections rather than sixteen separate input wires. A scan briefly drives one row LOW and reads four columns with internal pull-ups. A pressed key on that row pulls its column LOW. All inactive rows remain INPUT, so they are high impedance rather than actively driven HIGH. This avoids opposing output levels if more than one key creates a connection between rows. The lookup array turns a detected intersection into a printed character. Think of scanning as asking one row a question at a time. A column reading has meaning only together with the currently selected row. Release that row before selecting the next one, and keep its output latch LOW so INPUT does not enable a pull-up on the inactive row. The brief settling interval is deliberate bounded work, not a promise of zero blocking time. Printed key labels are software mappings; they cannot repair an unknown connector order. Establish the physical conductor map first, then check the lookup table.

  1. With power disconnected, connect the four rows and four columns as shown in the two wiring figures. The drawings describe logical conductors, not the order of the ribbon contacts.
  2. Upload the example and press each printed key individually. Record any key whose reported label differs from its face; inspect the row/column assignment before changing the lookup table.
  3. Release the key and observe RELEASED. This first sketch reports raw changes, so contact bounce may create extra lines. MULTIPLE means that scan found more than one low intersection, not a valid menu choice.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const byte rowPins[4] = {2, 3, 4, 5};
const byte colPins[4] = {6, 7, 8, 9};
const char labels[4][4] = {
  {'1','2','3','A'}, {'4','5','6','B'},
  {'7','8','9','C'}, {'*','0','#','D'}
};
void setupKeypad() {
  for (byte i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
    pinMode(rowPins[i], INPUT);
    pinMode(colPins[i], INPUT_PULLUP);
  }
}
// 0 = released, '!' = more than one detected key, else a key label.
char scanKeypad() {
  byte hits = 0;
  char found = 0;
  for (byte r = 0; r < 4; ++r) {
    digitalWrite(rowPins[r], LOW);
    pinMode(rowPins[r], OUTPUT);
    delayMicroseconds(5);  // Brief settling time before reading columns.
    for (byte c = 0; c < 4; ++c) {
      if (digitalRead(colPins[c]) == LOW) {
        ++hits;
        found = labels[r][c];
      }
    }
    pinMode(rowPins[r], INPUT);  // Release this row before the next.
  }
  if (hits == 0) return 0;
  return hits == 1 ? found : '!';
}
char previous = '?';
void setup() {
  setupKeypad();
  Serial.begin(9600);
}
void loop() {
  char reading = scanKeypad();
  if (reading != previous) {
    previous = reading;
    if (reading == 0) Serial.println("RELEASED");
    else if (reading == '!') Serial.println("MULTIPLE");
    else Serial.println(reading);
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Every single key should report its own label, and every release should eventually report RELEASED.
  • At the end of every scan, all four row pins are returned to INPUT.

Experiment

  • If the entire second and third rows report each other’s labels, which connections or mapping entries would you inspect first?

Debounced Press Events

Task 2 · Guided build

Choose one snack with one tap

A raw scan result is a level, not yet a trustworthy press event. The event helper restarts a timer whenever the candidate changes, then requires 25 ms unchanged. It arms only after all keys have been released for that interval. One accepted key disarms it until another stable release. This prevents a held key, a slide directly to another key, or a key held during startup from repeatedly selecting items. Observing multiple keys immediately disarms the helper. Unsigned elapsed-time subtraction keeps these short waits valid across millis rollover. The helper returns character value zero when there is no event. That value is different from the printed digit character 0. Application code should call the helper once per loop pass and distribute that single event to its decision logic, rather than scanning separately for each menu branch. An ignored application key still consumes its accepted press, so another action requires a release. Debouncing improves event interpretation but does not turn a diode-less matrix into a reliable multi-key device or validate it for security use.

  1. Reuse Task 1 wiring. Upload this example with no keys held, then leave the keypad released for at least 25 ms. No external Keypad library is required.
  2. Tap 1 for FRUIT, 2 for CRACKERS or 3 for YOGURT. Other keys are ignored. Each selection is one line in Serial Monitor; holding a key should not produce more lines.
  3. Restart with a key held, then release and tap again. Also try a very brief tap: an input that does not remain stable for 25 ms may be ignored.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const byte rowPins[4] = {2, 3, 4, 5};
const byte colPins[4] = {6, 7, 8, 9};
const char labels[4][4] = {
  {'1','2','3','A'}, {'4','5','6','B'},
  {'7','8','9','C'}, {'*','0','#','D'}
};
void setupKeypad() {
  for (byte i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
    pinMode(rowPins[i], INPUT);
    pinMode(colPins[i], INPUT_PULLUP);
  }
}
// 0 = released, '!' = more than one detected key, else a key label.
char scanKeypad() {
  byte hits = 0;
  char found = 0;
  for (byte r = 0; r < 4; ++r) {
    digitalWrite(rowPins[r], LOW);
    pinMode(rowPins[r], OUTPUT);
    delayMicroseconds(5);  // Brief settling time before reading columns.
    for (byte c = 0; c < 4; ++c) {
      if (digitalRead(colPins[c]) == LOW) {
        ++hits;
        found = labels[r][c];
      }
    }
    pinMode(rowPins[r], INPUT);  // Release this row before the next.
  }
  if (hits == 0) return 0;
  return hits == 1 ? found : '!';
}
char candidate = '!';
bool armed = false;
unsigned long candidateAt = 0;
char pressEvent(unsigned long now) {
  char reading = scanKeypad();
  if (reading != candidate) {
    candidate = reading;
    candidateAt = now;
  }
  if (reading == '!') {
    armed = false;
    return 0;
  }
  if (now - candidateAt < 25UL) return 0;
  if (reading == 0) {
    armed = true;
    return 0;
  }
  if (armed) {
    armed = false;
    return reading;
  }
  return 0;
}
void setup() {
  setupKeypad();
  Serial.begin(9600);
  candidate = scanKeypad();
  candidateAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  char key = pressEvent(millis());
  if (key == '1') Serial.println("FRUIT");
  else if (key == '2') Serial.println("CRACKERS");
  else if (key == '3') Serial.println("YOGURT");
}

Observe and check

  • A held key selects once, and a held-at-start key does not select until released and pressed again.
  • The 25 ms interval is an exercise setting, not a guarantee for every membrane switch or scanning speed.

Experiment

  • Why must a release become stable before the next press can be accepted?

Coordinate Mapping

Task 3 · Guided build

Audit a keypad label map

An unexpected label can come from a misplaced conductor or from the lookup table. Printing both the detected coordinate and its label separates those possibilities. This diagnostic keeps the raw scanner from teaching task 1 and records the row and column whenever it sees a contact. Coordinates are stored only for reporting a single detected key; a MULTIPLE scan is not presented as one trustworthy location. Array indices begin at zero while the printed functional conductor names begin at one, so the diagnostic adds one only for the human-readable output. Press one key at a time and compare all four corners before checking the interior. If an entire row appears shifted, revisit the physical row assignment with power disconnected instead of swapping isolated character labels until the display looks right. That workaround could conceal the wiring error and make future maintenance harder. This diagnostic still reports raw transitions and may show bounce.

  1. Upload the complete coordinate diagnostic on the existing keypad wiring.
  2. Check corners, then other keys individually; power off before correcting conductors.
Arduino sketch · guided example
byte detectedRow = 0, detectedColumn = 0;
const byte rowPins[4] = {2, 3, 4, 5};
const byte colPins[4] = {6, 7, 8, 9};
const char labels[4][4] = {
  {'1','2','3','A'}, {'4','5','6','B'},
  {'7','8','9','C'}, {'*','0','#','D'}
};
void setupKeypad() {
  for (byte i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
    pinMode(rowPins[i], INPUT);
    pinMode(colPins[i], INPUT_PULLUP);
  }
}
// 0 = released, '!' = more than one detected key, else a key label.
char scanKeypad() {
  byte hits = 0;
  char found = 0;
  for (byte r = 0; r < 4; ++r) {
    digitalWrite(rowPins[r], LOW);
    pinMode(rowPins[r], OUTPUT);
    delayMicroseconds(5);  // Brief settling time before reading columns.
    for (byte c = 0; c < 4; ++c) {
      if (digitalRead(colPins[c]) == LOW) {
        ++hits;
        found = labels[r][c];
        detectedRow = r; detectedColumn = c;
      }
    }
    pinMode(rowPins[r], INPUT);  // Release this row before the next.
  }
  if (hits == 0) return 0;
  return hits == 1 ? found : '!';
}
char previous = '?';
void setup() {
  setupKeypad();
  Serial.begin(9600);
}
void loop() {
  char reading = scanKeypad();
  if (reading != previous) {
    previous = reading;
    if (reading == 0) Serial.println("RELEASED");
    else if (reading == '!') Serial.println("MULTIPLE");
    else {
      Serial.print("R"); Serial.print(detectedRow + 1);
      Serial.print(" C"); Serial.print(detectedColumn + 1);
      Serial.print(" label="); Serial.println(reading);
    }
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Coordinates and printed characters expose different mapping stages.

Experiment

  • Describe the pattern expected if two complete column wires are swapped.

Events Versus Repeated Levels

Task 4 · Guided build

Count deliberate desk actions

The event helper and an application counter have different responsibilities. The helper decides when one deliberate press is accepted; the counter stores how many accepted presses have occurred. This sketch counts every valid single-key event, including keys that a particular menu might otherwise ignore. It caps the diagnostic count at 999 so a long-running test cannot wrap the displayed number back to zero. A held key should increase the count once, and a slide directly from one key to another should not add a second event without a stable all-key release. Compare this behavior with the raw-change report from teaching task 1. Several raw changes can correspond to one accepted action, and no new raw change while held does not mean the scanner stopped running. Call pressEvent only once in each loop. Using two separate calls for two decisions can consume the same evolving helper state inconsistently.

  1. Upload and compare taps, a long hold, and a fresh release followed by another tap.
  2. Keep all keys released for at least 25 ms between intended actions.

}

Observe and check

  • A long hold is one action, not a count of scans.

Experiment

  • Explain what the cap protects even if no one normally makes 999 presses.

Digit Characters and Available Values

Task 5 · Guided build

Remember a supply-drawer number

A key label is a character, not automatically the number written on its face. Once a key is known to lie between the characters 0 and 9, subtracting the character 0 converts it to the corresponding small integer. Validate the character range before this arithmetic. The drawer example must support drawer zero, so numeric zero cannot also mean no stored choice. A separate haveDrawer flag represents availability. The star key clears availability without needing to invent a special drawer number. The hash key reports the current drawer without consuming it, making repeated reports intentional here. This differs from an order-confirmation interface that clears a pending choice after use. Keeping those contracts explicit prevents the same state variables from quietly changing meaning across applications. Ignored keys do not alter the stored value. Reset returns to no stored drawer even though the numeric storage variable is initialized to zero.

  1. Upload, select digit 0, and request it with #.
  2. Clear with * and request again to compare missing and zero.

  Serial.begin(9600);
  candidate = scanKeypad();
  candidateAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  char key = pressEvent(millis());
  if (key >= '0' && key <= '9') {
    drawer = key - '0';
    haveDrawer = true;
    Serial.println("STORED");
  } else if (key == '*') {
    haveDrawer = false;
    Serial.println("CLEARED");
  } else if (key == '#') {
    if (haveDrawer) {
      Serial.print("DRAWER "); Serial.println(drawer);
    } else Serial.println("NONE");
  }
}

Observe and check

  • A legitimate zero remains distinguishable from no selection.

Experiment

  • Explain why # intentionally preserves this drawer selection.

Bounded Numeric Entry

Task 6 · Guided build

Edit a small tray quantity

Building a multi-digit number is an operation on state. Multiplying the previous number by ten shifts its decimal places, then adding the new digit appends that digit. This task accepts at most two digits, so the value remains between zero and 99. The digit count is still necessary: an empty entry and an entered zero have the same numeric value but different editing states. Leading zeros also consume input positions even though numeric output does not preserve their appearance. The D key removes the final digit by integer division by ten and decreases the digit count. At an empty entry it reports EMPTY instead of underflowing an unsigned counter. The star key clears both values. A third digit reports FULL without changing the draft. These are input-buffer rules, not physical dispensing commands. Describe each boundary before coding it and test sequences that include zero, backspace at empty, and extra digits.

  1. Upload and enter a two-digit draft, then remove its digits individually.
  2. Compare empty input with a single zero and try a third digit.

};

    pinMode(colPins[i], INPUT_PULLUP);
  }

    for (byte c = 0; c < 4; ++c) {

        ++hits;
        found = labels[r][c];
      }

    pinMode(rowPins[r], INPUT);  // Release this row before the next.

char candidate = '!';
bool armed = false;
unsigned long candidateAt = 0;
char pressEvent(unsigned long now) {
  char reading = scanKeypad();
  if (reading != candidate) {
    candidate = reading;
    candidateAt = now;
  }
  if (reading == '!') {

byte number = 0, digits = 0;
void setup() {
  setupKeypad();
  Serial.begin(9600);
  candidate = scanKeypad();
  candidateAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  char key = pressEvent(millis());
  if (key >= '0' && key <= '9') {
    if (digits < 2) {
      number = number * 10 + key - '0';
      ++digits;
      Serial.print("ENTRY "); Serial.println(number);
    } else Serial.println("FULL");
  } else if (key == 'D') {
    if (digits > 0) {
      number /= 10;
      --digits;
      Serial.println("BACKSPACE");
    } else Serial.println("EMPTY");
  } else if (key == '*') {
    number = 0; digits = 0;
    Serial.println("CLEARED");
  } else if (key == '#') {
    if (digits > 0) { Serial.print("DRAFT "); Serial.println(number); }
    else Serial.println("EMPTY");
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Digit count records editing state independently of the displayed numeric value.

Experiment

  • Predict the state after 0, 0, D, 7.

Context-Dependent Menus

Task 7 · Guided build

Choose an activity then its length

The meaning of a key can depend on the current page. This menu first accepts A for reading or B for drawing. Only after that choice do keys 1 and 2 select a short or long session. The enum declaration supplies readable names for the three page states; it does not introduce another electrical input. Keeping page state separate from the event character makes it clear why pressing 1 at the initial page does nothing. After reporting a complete activity choice, the program returns to the initial page. Star returns there from any page. Other keys are ignored according to the current context, and every accepted physical press still follows the same release rule. This sketch prints a plan only; it does not start a real timer. A simple transition table can expose missing cases before they become confusing interface behavior, especially cancellation and irrelevant keys.

  1. Upload and try both activity paths.
  2. Press 1 before choosing an activity, then cancel a partly chosen plan with *.

};

    pinMode(colPins[i], INPUT_PULLUP);
  }
}

    for (byte c = 0; c < 4; ++c) {

        found = labels[r][c];

  char reading = scanKeypad();
  if (reading != candidate) {
    candidate = reading;
    candidateAt = now;

  return 0;

enum Page { CHOOSE, READING, DRAWING };
Page page = CHOOSE;
void setup() {
  setupKeypad();
  Serial.begin(9600);
  candidate = scanKeypad();
  candidateAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  char key = pressEvent(millis());
  if (key == '*') { page = CHOOSE; Serial.println("CHOOSE ACTIVITY"); }
  else if (page == CHOOSE) {
    if (key == 'A') { page = READING; Serial.println("READING: 1 SHORT, 2 LONG"); }
    else if (key == 'B') { page = DRAWING; Serial.println("DRAWING: 1 SHORT, 2 LONG"); }
  } else if (key == '1' || key == '2') {
    Serial.print(page == READING ? "READING " : "DRAWING ");
    Serial.println(key == '1' ? "SHORT" : "LONG");
    page = CHOOSE;
  }
}

Observe and check

  • The same physical key has meaning only in the stated page context.

Experiment

  • List all states from which cancellation should return to the initial page.

Recovery and Input Traces

Task 8 · Explore and measure

Test release, bounce and ambiguous scans

An event detector should be tested with sequences, not just isolated key labels. Use the unchanged snack-selector sketch from teaching task 2. First observe a normal stable release followed by one press; then compare a held-at-start key and a press shorter than the acceptance interval. On paper, trace a multiple-contact marker followed by a stable single key without a release. The immediate disarming rule means that a stable all-key release is still required before another event. This prevents recovery from an ambiguous scan from selecting an unintended item. Distinguish that release history from application inactivity: a menu can be idle for seconds while a key remains held, yet still be unarmed. An inactivity message in a later application would use a separate timestamp of accepted events, not the candidate debounce timestamp. Give explicit event-versus-timeout priority if both occur on one loop pass. None of these logic tests establishes multi-key rollover or secure input behavior.

  1. Upload teaching task 2 unchanged and compare normal, held-start and very brief presses.
  2. Trace the ambiguous-scan sequence on paper instead of treating multiple keys as supported input.

Observe and check

  • Stable release is a required recovery step, not merely elapsed time.

Experiment

  • Specify which should win if a new event arrives exactly when an inactivity interval ends.
